extracted.intended_audience: educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, policymakers, and other stakeholders involved in Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and Department responses to public comments on the July 2022 NPRM for Title IX implementing regulations, focusing on definitions (e.g., complainant, administrative law judge), scope, grievance procedures, and dismissal/retroactivity rules to guide recipients' compliance and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.1 Purpose — scope and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose section of the regulations should state Title IX's nondiscrimination goal and include references to statutory exceptions; the phrase 'of the Education Amendments of 1972' need not be inserted and the reference to recipients other than educational institutions should be retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines requests to remove references to statutory exceptions because they are an important component of the statute (20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(1)-(9)). The Department also declines to insert Title IX's full statutory name; 'Title IX' is defined elsewhere (§106.2) to include the statute and amendments. Language recognizing that recipients beyond traditional educational institutions (e.g., libraries, hospitals) are covered should remain because such entities may offer education programs or activities subject to Title IX (cites to 20 U.S.C. 1681(a) and 1687 and historical preamble). Changes: none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Administrative Law Judge' (§106.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory definition of 'administrative law judge' refers to hearings held under §106.81 (the Department's compliance/enforcement hearing) and does not require that recipient-level Title IX grievance procedures include a hearing or participation by an administrative law judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that a hearing under §106.81 is distinct from any hearing conducted under recipient grievance procedures (§§106.45 or 106.46). Neither §106.45 nor §106.46 requires a live hearing or an ALJ's participation. Changes: none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Complainant' — who may file (§106.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'complainant' may be someone who is not currently a student or employee so long as that person was 'participating or attempting to participate' in the recipient's education program or activity at the time of the alleged sex discrimination; the definition intentionally omits the term 'victim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: The broadened definition remedies limitations from the 2020 amendments that required participation at the time of filing, which prevented complaints from prospective, former, or otherwise non-current participants. It is intended to encourage reporting (many survivors delay disclosure) and to ensure accountability for conduct that affected participation. Practical effect: recipients should proceed with such complaints under their usual grievance procedures (§§106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46). Limits/clarifications: the Department will not apply the final regulations retroactively; a complaint may be dismissed if the respondent is no longer participating or employed (§106.45(d)(1)(ii)) or if proven allegations would not constitute sex discrimination under Title IX or this part. The Dept. declined to make the provision retroactive and declined to categorically list every possible covered person (e.g., postdocs), noting such individuals may fall within student/employee/other categories depending on facts. Changes: minor textual edits to clarify timing language in §106.45(a)(2)(iv)(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation or 'attempting to participate' requirement (timing and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an individual was 'participating or attempting to participate' requires a fact-specific, case-by-case analysis measured at the time of the alleged sex discrimination (not at the time a complaint is filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include prospective students, guest speakers, visiting student-athletes, attendees at campus tours, sporting events, or lectures. The Department rejects narrowing the term to 'applying' as too limited. Purpose: the participation requirement prevents a recipient from being obligated to initiate grievance procedures for persons with no relationship to the recipient while ensuring Title IX protection for those who were engaged with the recipient's programs or activities when discrimination occurred. The Department cites case law (e.g., Doe v. Brown University; Snyder-Hill v. Ohio State Univ.) supporting coverage of non-students who were participating or attempting to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance procedures — 'prompt and equitable' resolution for all sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must adopt grievance procedures that provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of all complaints of sex discrimination (not limited to sexual harassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations require recipients to implement grievance procedures under which complaints of any form of sex discrimination are promptly and equitably resolved, and to take other necessary steps to maintain an educational environment free from sex discrimination. This aligns with longstanding regulatory requirements and is within the Department's authority to effectuate Title IX's purpose. The Department emphasizes that this obligation extends beyond harassment to all sex discrimination covered by Title IX and the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal standards for complaints (§106.45) — defined bases rather than vague 'specific circumstances'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed the 2020 amendments' vague 'specific circumstances' dismissal standard and revised §106.45 to include several defined bases for discretionary dismissal (for example, when the respondent is no longer participating or employed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, at the time the complaint is filed, the respondent is no longer participating in the recipient's education program or activity or is no longer employed by the recipient, the complaint may be dismissed under §106.45(d)(1)(ii). A complaint may also be dismissed if the allegations, even if proven, would not constitute sex discrimination under Title IX or this part (§106.45(d)(iv)). The Department explains it prefers defined dismissal bases to eliminate vagueness and to provide clearer guidance to recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-retroactivity of final regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations are intended to apply prospectively and not retroactively; they will not require recipients to apply regulatory requirements that were not in effect at the time of the alleged conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal basis: agencies generally lack authority to issue retroactive rules absent express statutory grant (citing 5 U.S.C. 551(4) and Bowen v. Georgetown Univ. Hosp.). Practically, if a complainant files a complaint seeking compliance solely with requirements not in effect when the conduct occurred, the recipient would dismiss the complaint. The Department therefore will not enforce new obligations retroactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'complainant' and concerns about increased complaints and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department acknowledges commenters' concerns that broadening the complainant definition and other regulatory changes could increase the volume of complaints and administrative burdens, but finds the broadened definition justified to ensure Title IX's nondiscrimination objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes potential increases in reporting due to including former participants, expanded coverage (e.g., gender identity, off-campus conduct), removal of the actual knowledge standard, and mandatory reporting by employees in some contexts. It accepts that recipients may incur additional administrative costs, but concludes that ensuring recipients address all sex discrimination under their programs or activities is paramount. For further cost analysis, see the Regulatory Impact Analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of volunteers and trainees within complainant coverage (fact-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteers, postdoctoral trainees, fellows, and others training under recipient institutions may be considered complainants if they were participating or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity at the time of the alleged discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to categorically state that specific categories (e.g., postdocs) are complainants but noted such individuals could fall within the definition as students, employees, or other persons participating or attempting to participate. The participation analysis remains fact-specific; including volunteers is intended to protect all 'persons' under 20 U.S.C. 1681(a). The Department rejects the argument that including volunteers will hinder recruitment, stating protection should aid recruitment and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-stigmatizing terminology in definitions (omit 'victim')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department intentionally omitted the term 'victim' from the definition of 'complainant' to avoid stigmatizing language and to promote reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters appreciated not using 'victim'; the Department noted omission may encourage reporting and avoid harmful language. This is a stylistic and policy choice embedded in the regulatory text to influence how complainants are characterized and treated.
